1. Which of the following defines a class in OOP?

a. A loop that repeats code

b. A blueprint for creating objects

c. A method of abstraction

d. A library of functions

Answer: b. A blueprint for creating objects

Remember: Classes define the structure and behavior of objects.

2. In OOP, what do we call the real-world entity created from a class?

a. Method

b. Object

c. Variable

d. Function

Answer: b. Object

Remember: Objects are instances of classes, representing real-world entities.

3. Which of these is NOT an OOP principle?

a. Inheritance

b. Encapsulation

c. Polymorphism

d. Compilation

Answer: d. Compilation

Remember: Compilation is part of program execution, not an OOP concept.

4. What does Encapsulation mean in OOP?

a. Wrapping data and methods together

b. Using many functions and once

c. Breaking code into similar parts

d. Writing loops inside a class

Answer: a. Wrapping data and methods together

Remember: Encapsulation hides data and bundles it with methods.

5. In c++, which access modifier makes a class member visible everywhere?

a. private

b. public

c. protected

d. internal

Answer: b. Public

Remember: public allows unrestricted access across the program.

1. Given the code snippet below, what will be the output?

class Animal {
  public virtual void Sound() {
    Console.WriteLine("Animal sound");
  }
}

class Dog : Animal {
  public override void Sound() {
    Console.WriteLine("Bark");
  }
}

class Program {
  static void Main(string[ ] args) {
    Animal myDog = new Dog();
    myDog.Sound();
  }
}

a. Animal sound

b. Bark

c. Error in compilation

d. No output

Answer: b. bark

Remember: Polymorphism allows myDog.Sound() to use the Dog implementation.

2. Which access modifier allows a class member to be accessible only within its class and derived classes?

a. private

b. protected

c. public

d. internal

Answer: b. protected

Remember: protected allows access within the same class and subclasses

3.What will happen if you create an object of an abstract class in C++?

a. It will compile successfully.

b. It will cause a runtime error.

c. It will cause a compilation error.

d. It will create an empty object.

Answer: c. It will cause a compilation error

Remember: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated.

4. In C++, which of the following best demonstrates encapsulation?

a. Declaring a variable as public

b. Grouping methods and variables inside a class and making them private

c. Overriding a method in a child class

d. Writing methods with the same name but different parameters

Answer: b. Grouping methods and variables inside a class and making them private

Remember: Encapsulation hides implementation and protects data.

5.Suppose you created a generic class Box. What does represent?

a. A type parameter that can be replaced with any data type

b. A constant value for a class

c. A loop variable

d. A default C++ type

Answer: a. A type parameter that can be replaced with any data type

Remember: Generics allow defining a class with placeholders for data types.

1. Debugging scenario: What will be the output of the following code? 

class A {
  public virtual void Show() {
    Console.WriteLine("Class A");
  }
}
class B : A {
  public override void Show() {
    Console.WriteLine("Class B");
  }
}
class C : B {
  public new void Show() {
    Console.WriteLine("Class C");
  }
}
class Program {
  static void Main() {
    A obj = new C();
    obj.Show();
  }
}

a. Class A

b. Class B

c. Class C

d. Error

Answer: b. Class B

Remember: new hides method in C, but since obj is type A, it calls the overridden method in B.

2.Which of the following situations BEST demonstrates polymorphism in C++?

a. Having multiple classes share a single base class.

b. A subclass overriding a parent class method with its own implementation.

c. Creating multiple objects of the same class.

d. Declaring private variables inside a class.

Answer: b. A subclass overriding a parent class method with its own implementation.

Remember: This is method overriding, runtime polymorphism.

3.Consider this code snippet and define what is the output:

List numbers = new List(){1,2,3,4,5};
var result = numbers.Where(n => n % 2 == 0).ToList();
Console.WriteLine(result[0]);

a. 1

b. 2

c. 4

d. Error

Answer: b. 2

Remember: LINQ filters even numbers, [2,4]. First element is 2.

4.Which of the following is the MOST accurate statement about interfaces in C++?

a. Interfaces can contain both implementation and declarations.

b. A class can inherit only one interface.

c. Interfaces support multiple inheritance of type definitions.

d. Interfaces are slower than classes and not recommended.

Answer: c. Interfaces support multiple inheritance of type definitions.

Remember: A class can implement multiple interfaces in C#.

5.You are tasked to design a program using encapsulation. Which of the following best applies it?

a. Creating private fields and exposing them through public properties.

b. Writing a method with the same name in different classes.

c. Creating multiple constructors with different parameters.

d. Using an abstract method inside an abstract class.

Answer: a. Creating private fields and exposing them through public properties.

Remember: Encapsulation = data hiding + controlled access.

Course Objectives

- CO1. Define the four OOP concepts--Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, and Polymorphism.

- CO2. Apply the four OOP concepts by writing basic C++ class structures, member functions, and simple program implementations.

- CO3. Analyze C++ code to identify correct and incorrect uses of Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, and Polymorphism.

- CO4. Evaluate different C++ program designs by comparing how effectively they implement the four OOP concepts.

- CO5. Create a functional C++ program that integrates all four OOP concepts to solve a defined programming task.

- CO6. Design and write a software application applying OOP concept based on a given problem/situation.

- CO7. Develop an application/software based system as a team to accomplish a given problem.

- CO8. Explains object-oriented programming (OOP) principles and their benefit in developing real-world applications

- CO9. Describe the purpose of collections, and explain how to use generics to implement type-safe collection classes, structures, interfaces, and methods.

- CO10. Demonstrate an understanding in the technological progress and emerging trends in device programming

What is Inheritance?

In Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), inheritance is a mechanism where a new class (derived class) acquires properties and behaviors from an existing class (base class). This promotes code reusability by allowing derived classes to inherit common attributes and functions, rather than duplicating them. The derived class can then extend or modify the inherited features, creating a specialized version of the base class.

Why is Inheritance important?

Promotes code reusability, no need to repeat code.

Makes programs organized and maintainable.

Real-world example:

Parent Class: Vehicle = can start, can stop.

Child Class: Car = inherits start/stop, and adds drive.

C++ Code Example:
    #include 

    using namespace std;

    class Vehicle {
    public:
        void start() {
            cout << "Vehicle starting..." << endl;
        }

    };

    class Car : public Vehicle {  // Inherits from Vehicle

    public:
        void drive() {
            cout << "Car is driving..." << endl;
        }
    };


    int main() {
        Car myCar;
        myCar.start();  // Inherited
        myCar.drive();  // Car-specific
        return 0;
    }
Output:

Vehicle is starting...

Car is Driving...

Key points to remember:

Use : to show inheritance (class Car : public Vehicle).

Derived classes reuse methods of base classes.

Derived classes can add their own features.

What is Encapsulation?

Encapsulation in OOP is the process of bundling data (attributes) and the methods (functions) that operate on that data into a single unit, typically a class. It involves hiding the internal state of an object and controlling access to it through public methods (like getters and setters), thereby protecting the data from unauthorized modification and ensuring data integrity.

Why is Encapsulation important?

- Provides

- Prevents accidental changes to variables

- Makes program more secure and reliable

C++ Code Example:
    #include 
    using namespace std;

    class Account {
    private:
        double balance;   // hidden data

    public:
        // setter method
        void setBalance(double b) {
            if (b >= 0) balance = b;  // validation
        }
        // getter method
        double getBalance() {
            return balance;
        }
    };

    int main() {
        Account myAcc;
        myAcc.setBalance(5000);   // access via method
        cout << "Balance: " << myAcc.getBalance() << endl;
        return 0;
    }
Output:

Vehicle is starting...

Car is Driving...

Key points to remember:

Use : to show inheritance (class Car : public Vehicle).

Derived classes reuse methods of base classes.

Derived classes can add their own features.

Focus on what matters; hide what doesn’t

What is Abstraction?

In object-oriented programming (OOP), abstraction is the process of hiding complex internal implementation details and displaying only the essential, relevant features of an object to the user or other programs. It simplifies complex systems by showing only the important functionality, reducing complexity and increasing efficiency.

Why is Abstraction important?

- Reduces complexity by hiding details. (CO4)

- Focuses only on what is needed. (CO6)

- Makes code easier to maintain and extend. (CO8)

C++ Code Example:
    #include 
    using namespace std;

    // Abstract class
    class Shape {
    public:
        virtual void draw() = 0;  // Pure virtual function
    };
    class Circle : public Shape {
    public:
        void draw() {
            cout << "Drawing a Circle" << endl;
        }
    };

    int main() {
        Shape* s = new Circle();
        s->draw();   // Calls Circle's implementation
        delete s;
        return 0;
    }
Output:

Vehicle is starting...

Car is Driving...

Key points to remember:

Use : to show inheritance (class Car : public Vehicle).

Derived classes reuse methods of base classes.

Derived classes can add their own features.

Flexibility is the key to stability.

What is Polymorphism?

Polymorphism in Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is the ability of objects to take on multiple forms or behaviors, allowing different objects to be treated as instances of a common parent class while retaining their unique implementations. This core OOP concept enables code to be more flexible, reusable, and maintainable by providing a single interface to diverse underlying classes, making programs adaptable to new situations and easier to manage.

Types of Polymorphism?

- Compile-time (Static) → Function overloading, operator overloading.

- Run-time (Dynamic) → Achieved using virtual functions.

C++ Code Example:
    #include 
    using namespace std;

    class Animal {
    public:
        virtual void makeSound() {
            cout << "Some generic animal sound" << endl;
        }
    };
    int main() {
        Animal* a1 = new Dog();
        Animal* a2 = new Cat();

        a1->makeSound();  // Calls Dog’s version
        a2->makeSound();  // Calls Cat’s version

        delete a1;
        delete a2;
        return 0;
    }
Output:

Barking...

Meowing...

Key points to remember:

Polymorphism - one interface, multiple implementations.

Achieved in C++ by virtual functions (dynamic binding).

Increases flexibility and reusability of code.

    class Cat : public Animal {
    public:
        void speak()  { cout << "Meow"; }             
        // (2) Fill in
    };

Easy

- This post-test has 8 items (2 questions per OOP pillar).

- Read each question carefully and select the best answer.

- There is no time limit.

- You may use the hint button if needed (no penalty in Easy Level).

- At the end, you will see your score and earn a badge for completion.

- It is your requirement to finish the post-test.

Easy

1. What does inheritance allow in Object-Oriented Programming?

a. One class to hide data from another

b. One class to acquire attributes and behaviors of another

c. One method to perform multiple tasks

d. One class to contain only abstract methods

Answer: b. One class to acquire attributes and behaviors of another

Remember: Inheritance allows a derived class to reuse properties and methods of a base class.

2.Which symbol is used in C++ to declare inheritance?

a. :

b. ;

c. {}

d. ()

Answer: a. :

Remember: class Child : public Parent uses : for inheritance.

3.Which keyword in C++ is used to hide data inside a class?

a. public

b. private

c. protected

d. static

Answer: b. private

Remember: private restricts access to data members.

4. Which method allows controlled access to private data?

a. getter and setter methods

b. loops and conditions

c. constructors

d. headers

Answer: a. getter and setter methods

Remember: Encapsulation uses getter/setter methods to safely access private data.

5. In C++, abstraction is implemented using:

a. Loops

b. Abstract classes and pure virtual functions

c. Templates

d. Constructors

Answer: b. Abstract classes and pure virtual functions

Remember: Abstraction hides implementation details using abstract classes and pure virtual functions.

6. What does declaring virtual void draw() = 0; mean?

a. The function is private

b. The function is overloaded

c. The function is a pure virtual function

d. The function is inline

Answer: c. The function is a pure virtual function

Remember: = 0 means pure virtual, no implementation in the base class.

7. What does polymorphism mean in Object-Oriented Programming?

a. One object can inherit many classes

b. One function can have multiple forms

c. One class can contain only public methods

d. One function can only be static

Answer: b. One function can have multiple forms

Remember: Polymorphism = “many forms”, function behaves differently depending on the object.

8. Which keyword in C++ enables runtime polymorphism?

a. abstract

b. protected

c. virtual

d. override

Answer: c. virtual

Remember: Declaring a function as virtual allows derived classes to override it at runtime.

Moderate

480

1. What will be the output?

class A {
public:
    void show() { cout << "Class A"; }
};
class B : public A {
public:
    void show() { cout << "Class B"; }
};
int main() {
    B obj;
    obj.show();
}

a. Class A

b. Class B

c. Error

d. Both A and B

Answer: b.

Remember: The show() method in B overrides A’s version. Since obj is of type B, Class B is displayed.

2. Fill in the blank to correctly inherit Car from Vehicle:

class Car ______ Vehicle { };

a. extends

b. : public

c. inherits

d. : protected

Answer: b.

Remember: C++ uses : public to show inheritance. extends is for Java, not C++.

3. Why is encapsulation important in C++ classes?

a. To allow direct access to variables.

b. To hide data and control access using methods.

c. To avoid creating objects.

d. To make functions global.

Answer: b.

Remember: Encapsulation hides sensitive data by using private members and controlling access via getters/setters.

4. What will the code output?

class Student {
private:
    int age;
public:
    void setAge(int a) { age = a; }
    int getAge() { return age; }
};

int main() {
    Student s;
    s.setAge(20);
    cout << s.getAge();
}

a. 0

b. 20

c. Error

d. Undefined

Answer: b.

Remember: The setter updates age to 20, and the getter retrieves it, so the output is 20.

5. Which makes a class abstract in C++?

a. To allow direct access to variables.

b. To hide data and control access using methods.

c. To avoid creating objects.

d. To make functions global.

Answer: c.

Remember: C++ does not use the abstract keyword. A class is abstract if it has at least one pure virtual function (= 0).

6. What happens if a derived class does not implement all pure virtual functions?

a. It becomes abstract itself

b. It compiles but errors at runtime

c. It implements them automatically

d. They are ignored

Answer: a.

Remember: If a derived class does not override pure virtual functions, it remains abstract and cannot be instantiated.

7. What is the output?

class Animal {
public:
    virtual void speak() { cout << "Animal"; }
};
class Dog : public Animal {
public:
    void speak() override { cout << "Dog"; }
};
int main() {
    Animal* a = new Dog();
    a->speak();
}

a. Animal

b. Dog

c. AnimalDog

d. Error

Answer: b.

Remember: Because of the virtual keyword, runtime polymorphism occurs. The pointer a calls Dog’s overridden function, so the output is Dog.

8. Function overloading in C++ is resolved at:

a. Runtime

b. Compile-time

c. Link-time

d. Execution-time

Answer: b.

Remember: Overloading (same function name, different parameters) is decided by the compiler — so it’s resolved at compile-time.

300

1. What is wrong with this code?

class Animal {
public:
    void speak() { cout << "Animal"; }
};
class Dog : public Animal {
public:
    void speak() override { cout << "Dog"; }
};

a. override cannot be used without virtual in base class

b. Missing semicolon after class Dog

c. Cannot inherit without protected

d. No error

Answer: a.

Remember: In C++, a function must be declared virtual in the base class before a derived function can use override.

2. Predict the output:

class Base {
public:
    Base() { cout << "Base "; }
};
class Derived : public Base {
public:
    Derived() { cout << "Derived"; }
};
int main() {
    Derived d;
}

a. Base Derived

b. Derived Base

c. Derived only

d. Error

Answer: a.

Remember: When creating a Derived object, the Base constructor runs first, then the Derived constructor.

3. Why does this code fail to compile?

class Student {
private:
    int age;
};
int main() {
    Student s;
    s.age = 20;
}

a. age is private and cannot be accessed directly

b. Missing constructor

c. No main function return type

d. Needs public inheritance

Answer: a.

Remember: age is declared private, so it cannot be accessed outside the class.

4. Which is the best way to securely set a salary variable??

a. Make salary public

b. Use a setter function that validates input

c. Use protected keyword

d. Assign directly in main

Answer: b.

Remember: Encapsulation means using setter functions to validate and safely update private variables.

5. Predict the output:

class Shape {
public:
    virtual void draw() = 0;
};
class Circle : public Shape {
public:
    void draw() { cout << "Circle"; }
};
int main() {
    Shape* s = new Circle();
    s->draw();
}

a. Error

b. Circle

c. Shape

d. Nothing

Answer: b.

Remember: Shape is abstract, but Circle implements draw(). A base pointer to a derived object calls Circle’s version.

6. What is wrong with this abstract class?

                            class Abstract {
public:
    virtual void display() = 0;
};
int main() {
    Abstract a;
}

a. Pure virtual functions need implementation

b. Cannot instantiate an abstract class

c. Missing semicolon

d. Needs inheritance

Answer: b.

Remember: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly. They require a derived class implementation.

7. Predict the output:

class Animal {
public:
    virtual void sound() { cout << "Animal"; }
};
class Cat : public Animal {
public:
    void sound() { cout << "Meow"; }
};
int main() {
    Animal a;
    a.sound();
}

a. Animal

b. Meow

c. Animal Meow

d. Meow

Answer: a.

Remember: a is a base object, not a pointer. Virtual dispatch does not apply here, it calls Animal’s method.

8. Why is this code wrong?

class Math {
public:
    int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
    float add(float a, float b) { return a + b; }
};
int main() {
    Math m;
    cout << m.add(5, 2.5);
}

a. Ambiguity in overloaded methods

b. Must declare virtual functions

c. Constructors missing

d. add() cannot be overloaded

Answer: a.

Remember: Passing 5 (int) and 2.5 (float) creates ambiguity between int add(int,int) and float add(float,float).

1. Fill in the missing keyword to correctly implement inheritance.

class Vehicle {
public:
    void drive() { cout << "Driving"; }
};

class Car ______ Vehicle {
public:
    void honk() { cout << "Beep!"; }
};

a. Class A

b. Class B

c. Class C

d. Error

Answer: b. A blueprint for creating objects

Remember: Classes define the structure and behavior of objects.

2. Fill in the missing keyword to protect data and access it safely.

class Account {
    ______:
        double balance;
    public:
        void setBalance(double b) { balance = b; }
};

a. private

b. protected

c. public

d. internal

Answer: b. Object

Remember: Objects are instances of classes, representing real-world entities.

class Shape {
public:
    virtual void draw() ______;
};

a. Inheritance

b. Encapsulation

c. Polymorphism

d. Compilation

Answer: d. Compilation

Remember: Compilation is part of program execution, not an OOP concept.

4. Complete the abstract class definition.

class Animal {
public:
    ______ void speak() { cout << "Animal"; }
};

class Dog : public Animal {
public:
    void speak() ______ { cout << "Bark"; }
};

a. Declaring a variable as public

b. Grouping methods and variables inside a class and making them private

c. Overriding a method in a child class

d. Writing methods with the same name but different parameters

Answer: a. Wrapping data and methods together

Remember: Encapsulation hides data and bundles it with methods.

5. Fill in the missing keyword to implement inheritance.

class Vehicle {
public:
    void drive() { cout << "Driving"; }
};

class Car ______ Vehicle {
public:
    void honk() { cout << "Beep!"; }
};

a. private

b. public

c. protected

d. internal

Answer: b. Public

Remember: public allows unrestricted access across the program.

6. Complete the constructor call for derived class.

class Base {
public:
    Base(int x) { cout << x; }
};
class Derived : public Base {
public:
    Derived(int y) : ______(y) { }
};

a. Declaring a variable as public

b. Grouping methods and variables inside a class and making them private

c. Overriding a method in a child class

d. Writing methods with the same name but different parameters

Answer: a. Wrapping data and methods together

Remember: Encapsulation hides data and bundles it with methods.

7. Fill in the missing keyword for data protection. 

class Account {
    ______:
        double balance;
public:
    void setBalance(double b) { balance = b; }
};

a. Declaring a variable as public

b. Grouping methods and variables inside a class and making them private

c. Overriding a method in a child class

d. Writing methods with the same name but different parameters

Answer: a. Wrapping data and methods together

Remember: Encapsulation hides data and bundles it with methods.

8. Which keyword allows controlled inheritance access?

class Student {
protected:
    int grade;
public:
    void setGrade(int g) { grade = g; }
};
class CollegeStudent ______ Student {
public:
    void display() { cout << grade; }
};

a. Declaring a variable as public

b. Grouping methods and variables inside a class and making them private

c. Overriding a method in a child class

d. Writing methods with the same name but different parameters

Answer: a. Wrapping data and methods together

Remember: Encapsulation hides data and bundles it with methods.
